e.etymology: A respelling of Brinley, an English surname from a place name usually explained as Old English for a burnt clearing. As a girls' name it rose in the 2010s with the -lee ending.
From the alder, a water-loving tree of the birch family, and from the surname given to someone who lived by alders. The word goes back to Old English alor.
A recent American coinage that joins the Ry- of Ryder and Rylan to the -o ending of Milo and Arlo, with an echo of Kylo from the Star Wars films.
French form of Henry, from the Germanic Heimirich, built from heim, 'home', and rih, 'ruler'. Four kings of France bore it.
namesakes: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec (French painter of Paris nightlife)

assoc.t: Tropical Storm Henri, which hit New England in 2021

e.etymology: From Arabic jamila, 'beautiful', the feminine of Jamil. It is used across the Muslim world and, since the 1970s, by African American families.
An African American coinage of the late 20th century that extends Javon with the -ion ending heard in Davion and Tavion.
A respelling of Blake, an English surname from Old English blaec, 'black, dark', or blac, 'pale, shining'; the two words fell together. This spelling is used mostly for girls.
From Sanskrit Rudra, the fierce storm god of the Rigveda and later a name of Shiva. It is usually explained as 'the roarer' or 'the howler', from the root rud, 'to cry, howl'.
A 19th-century coinage joining Lou, the short form of Louise, with the ending -ella. Luella is the other common spelling.
From an English surname taken from places such as Tineley in Northumberland. It entered the girls' top 1000 in 2010, the year Tenley Molzahn appeared on The Bachelor.
From Hindi diya, the small clay oil lamp lit at Diwali, from Sanskrit dipa, 'lamp'. A separate Arabic name, Diya, means 'radiance' and is given to boys.
Italian form of the Roman name Aetius, from Greek aetos, 'eagle'. Its recent American use follows Ezio Auditore, the Renaissance hero of the Assassin's Creed video games.

assoc.t: Ezio Auditore, hero of the Assassin's Creed games

e.etymology: From Hebrew ilan, 'tree', a word borrowed from Aramaic. It is a modern Israeli name, traditionally linked to Tu BiShvat, the new year of the trees.
namesakes: Ilan Ramon (Israeli astronaut lost aboard the shuttle Columbia)

e.etymology: A recent American name with no settled source, probably built on Amari with an added N. Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon (2021) has a warrior princess named Namaari.

assoc.t: Namaari, rival in Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon

e.etymology: A medieval reshaping of Amabel, from Latin amabilis, 'lovable', in use since the 12th century. It was later read as Anna plus belle, 'beautiful Anna'.
namesakes: Annabel Lee (lost love of Edgar Allan Poe's last poem)

assoc.t: Annabel Lee, the lost love in Poe's poem
Annabelle, haunted doll of the Conjuring horror films

e.etymology: The Manx form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. In the United States it is mostly used as a phonetic spelling of the Scottish Ian.
From an English surname and place name, Old English east plus tun, 'east settlement'. It shares that origin with Easton.

assoc.t: Aston Martin, British sports car of the Bond films
Aston Villa, English Premier League soccer club

e.meaning: to tie or bind (the traditional reading of Rivka)
e.etymology: Yiddish pet form of Rivka, the Hebrew original of Rebecca, wife of Isaac in Genesis. It is used mainly in Orthodox Jewish communities.

e.meaning: from the Roman family name Caecilius, possibly 'blind'
e.etymology: The medieval English form of Cecilia, from the Roman family name Caecilius, possibly from caecus, 'blind'. Saint Cecilia, a Roman martyr, is the patron saint of music.
namesakes: Cecily Strong (Saturday Night Live cast member)

e.etymology: From the most common surname in the English-speaking world, Old English smith, a worker in metal. It has been used as a first name since the 19th century, often to carry on a family surname.

assoc.t: the most common surname in the United States
Smith College, women's college in Massachusetts

e.note: Heard first as a last name, so expect it to be taken for a surname on forms and class lists.

e.etymology: A respelling of Carson, a Scottish surname of uncertain origin, sometimes read as 'son of Carr'. Carson became an American first name partly through frontiersman Kit Carson.

e.meaning: princess (as a Yiddish form of Sarah)
e.etymology: Several sources. In Yiddish it is a pet form of Sarah, Hebrew for 'princess'; in Persian suri is a red rose; in Sanskrit suri means 'learned'. Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes chose it for their daughter in 2006.

assoc.t: Suri Cruise, daughter of Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes
suri, a silky-fleeced breed of alpaca

e.note: Often misheard as Siri, Apple's voice assistant.

e.meaning: noble (through Alicia); also linked to the alyssum flower
e.etymology: A spelling of Alyssa, which grew out of Alicia, a Latinized form of Alice (from a Germanic name meaning 'noble kind'), with influence from the flower alyssum.
From the Latin name Marinus, 'of the sea'. In France and the Balkans it is a boys' name; American parents give it mostly to girls.

assoc.t: Marin County, north of San Francisco

e.meaning: born of the yew, or well-born
e.etymology: Anglicized form of Scottish Gaelic Eoghan, an old name read either as 'born of the yew' or as a Gaelic form of Eugene, 'well-born'. It is not related to the Welsh Evan.
namesakes: Ewan McGregor (Scottish actor, Obi-Wan Kenobi in Star Wars)

assoc.t: Ewan McGregor, Scottish actor of Star Wars and Trainspotting

e.etymology: A transliteration of Arabic Malik, which covers two related words: malik, 'king', and maalik, 'owner, master'. The spelling Malek is usual in North Africa and the Levant.
A modern American coinage in the family of Javion and Davion, opened with the fashionable Zay- sound. Zavion and Zaevion are other spellings.
From an English surname taken from places in Devon and Somerset, from Old English brant, 'steep', describing a hill. It became a first name in the 20th century.
namesakes: Brent Spiner (Data on Star Trek: The Next Generation)

assoc.t: Brent crude, the benchmark price of oil

e.etymology: A 20th-century American coinage joining Jay with the ending -lynn. It has many spellings, among them Jaelyn and Jaylin.
The Polish, Norwegian and Slovene spelling of Alexander, from Greek Alexandros: alexo, 'to defend', plus aner, 'man'. Alexander the Great carried the name across Europe and Asia.
From the English word and the surname given to someone who came from the west or lived west of a village. Parents also use it as a short form of Weston or Wesley.

assoc.t: the compass direction and the American West

e.etymology: From an English surname, a patronymic meaning 'son of Eade', a medieval given name. It is well liked by Chinese American families, helped by the Hong Kong singer Eason Chan.
